source.book: The Art and Science of Technical Analysis
source.author: Adam Grimes

conventions: stop and limit entries mechanized as bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; price-level conditions rejected (shift test)

rejected.quote: We are pattern recognition machines. Our brains are so good at recognizing patterns that they will readily create patterns where none exist.
rejected.reason: cognitive-bias description (pattern perception in randomness); pure discretion, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: Oh, they got my stop again. That guy screwed me again. Can you believe that?
rejected.reason: shifting-blame bias narrative; no bar-level test

rejected.quote: Stop trading. If you are a short-term trader, immediately exit any position that is showing a loss, and place breakeven or better stops on any other open trades.
rejected.reason: a concrete action checklist for being 'on tilt', but the trigger ('recognizing that you are there' / self-assessed anger and aggression) is subjective and not derivable from OHLCV or position-history data; no bar-level test for the trigger, so the whole protocol is rejected even though the response actions (stop trading, exit losers) would themselves be mechanizable if a real trigger existed

rejected.quote: The gambler's fallacy stems from faulty intuition about random processes... a trader might increase risk on trades after a string of losers.
rejected.reason: catalog of cognitive biases (gambler's fallacy, loss-aversion framing, overconfidence, confirmation, anchoring, recency, hindsight, illusion of control); psychological description of trader behavior, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: This is a problem for traders, because the market is like this teacher; it often rewards incorrect behaviors and punishes perfectly correct actions.
rejected.reason: random-reinforcement / sample-size argument; statistics-of-the-book material, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: For traders, fear and hope are the twin monsters, and no matter how experienced we may be as traders, we are unable to completely conquer them.
rejected.reason: emotional narrative (ego, hope, fear); no bar-level test

rejected.quote: Intuition is an important part of the trading process for many traders and styles of trading... it is a way of knowing that falls outside rational thought.
rejected.reason: discretionary/intuitive skill description; no bar-level test ('read the tape' category)

rejected.quote: In the flow state, we are supremely competent... Elite performers do their best work in the flow state.
rejected.reason: psychological performance-state description; no bar-level test

rejected.quote: Who are you? It has been said that if you don't know the answer to this question, the markets are an expensive place to find out.
rejected.reason: trader-development and business/style-choice guidance (market, time frame, discretionary vs. systematic); not a market condition, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: one of the most important keys to successful trading is consistency... remove degrees of freedom whenever possible.
rejected.reason: general behavioral advice on discipline and consistency; no bar-level test

chapter_summary: Chapter 11 is entirely psychological: cognitive biases, emotional control (ego, hope, fear), intuition, flow, and practical suggestions for developing self-directed traders. It produced no mechanizable candidates. The only quasi-actionable passage -- a checklist of what to do when 'on tilt' (stop trading, flatten losers, take a break) -- was rejected because the trigger (self-recognizing tilt) has no bar-level or position-history test; if a later pass wants to revisit it, the response actions themselves (force-flat, block entries) are straightforward Switch/Exit primitives once/if a trigger is defined.
